reference.source: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
clinicalPearls: Pleural plaques are discrete, well-circumscribed areas of hyaline (collagenous) fibrosis of the parietal pleura and are the commonest manifestation of asbestos exposure.
They characteristically involve the posterolateral chest wall, the domes of the diaphragm and the mediastinal pleura, while sparing the costophrenic angles and lung apices.
There is a long latency, typically 20 to 40 years from first exposure.
Plaques are usually asymptomatic incidental radiological findings and rarely cause meaningful functional impairment.
Calcification is common with time and aids radiological recognition.
They are a marker of asbestos exposure and hence of increased risk of other asbestos-related disease, but are not themselves premalignant and do not transform into mesothelioma.
CT is more sensitive and specific than chest radiography and helps separate plaques from mimics such as extrapleural fat.
Their main importance is as a marker of exposure prompting counselling on mesothelioma and lung cancer risk and on smoking cessation.
reference.pathophysiology: Inhaled asbestos fibres, particularly the longer amphibole fibres, are carried to the parietal pleura via lymphatic channels. There they incite a low-grade, chronic inflammatory and fibrogenic response with deposition of dense, relatively acellular basket-weave hyaline collagen, forming discrete plaques on the parietal pleura and diaphragm. Over years these plaques may calcify. Unlike diffuse pleural thickening and mesothelioma, plaques remain localised, typically spare the visceral pleura and reflect cumulative exposure rather than a progressive malignant process.
additionalDifferentials: Fibrothorax from healed empyema or haemothorax
Rib companion shadows and other plain-film mimics
additionalInvestigations: High-resolution CT of the thorax for characterisation and to exclude other disease
Pulmonary function tests (usually normal; to detect coexistent asbestosis)
Comparison with previous imaging to confirm stability
Further characterisation with PET or biopsy only if features suggest malignancy
redFlags: Pleural thickening that is nodular, circumferential or associated with a mass, raising concern for mesothelioma
Chest pain or unexplained weight loss
Progressive or asymmetric thickening on serial imaging
reference.prognosis: Pleural plaques themselves are benign with an excellent prognosis and rarely cause symptoms or meaningful functional impairment; their significance lies in signalling asbestos exposure and the associated lifetime risk of mesothelioma and lung cancer.
pitfalls: Misinterpreting plaques as metastases or mesothelioma, or vice versa.
Wrongly telling a patient that plaques turn into cancer, causing unnecessary alarm; they are markers, not precursors.
Confusing extrapleural fat or normal muscle shadows with plaques on plain films.
Failing to counsel on smoking cessation, which multiplies asbestos-related lung cancer risk.
Overlooking coexisting asbestosis or an early mesothelioma.
references: Murray & Nadel's Textbook of Respiratory Medicine
BTS Statement on Asbestos-related Pleural Disease
management: Reassure that pleural plaques are benign, rarely symptomatic and not themselves premalignant, requiring no disease-specific therapy
Confirm cessation of asbestos exposure and document a detailed occupational history to support medico-legal and compensation needs
Advise smoking cessation to reduce the compounded lifetime risk of lung cancer
Maintain vigilance for other asbestos-related disease, investigating any new breathlessness, chest pain or pleural effusion
Compare with previous imaging to confirm stability and exclude evolving diffuse pleural thickening or malignancy
Monitor pulmonary function to detect coexistent asbestosis
Refer for further imaging or biopsy only where features suggest malignant transformation elsewhere in the pleura
